endorsements.quote: Feedback must be triaged and analysed systematically by interdisciplinary teams, ensuring that concerns inform both technical refinement and organizational learning.

Finally, organizations should implement accessible and responsive user -centred feedback mechanisms that allow individuals to report concerns, share experiences, and raise ethical questions regarding AI use ( 37).

In this sense, pe riodic algorithmic audits should be mandated to evaluate bias, transparency, and alignment with person-centred principles (33,34), while deliberative forums ensure that oversight remains dialogical and value-driven rather than technocratic.

New governance structures, such as interdisciplinary cyber -bioethics boards or national commissions on digital health equity, are therefore required to assess not only performance and safety but also the relational, ethical, and experiential implication s of AI integration (32).
This includes creating platforms where people receiving care, caregivers, and health professionals participate in designing, evaluating, and adapting AI tools (30).

Mechanisms such as ethics committees or advisory panels, including diverse stakeholders, can help maintain accountability and ensure that AI supports rather than overrides human judgment and self-will (5,32,33).
In scheduling, as in clinical decision support, meaningful participation requires the ability to pause or amend algorithmic outcomes without penalty and with institutional backing.
Curricula should be updated to include AI competencies , human -machine collaboration, and person-centred communication in technology-rich contexts.
Maintaining clarity, explaining AI inputs in accessible language, and ensuring informed consent are essential to preserve trust and autonomy.
A promising line of argument is that AI can scaffold person-centredness when it is used to support, not substitute, clinical judgment and dialogue (39).

Leadership is critical in this process and must be supported through ongoing professional development that fosters informatics competencies, critical engagement with AI, ethical reasoning, and humanistic, person -centred practice.

unlisted_practices: Embed person-centred values and ethical commitments alongside efficiency goals directly into national policy documents and digital health strategies.

Develop and use person-centred indicators such as user collaboration, perceived dignity, participation in decision-making, and emotional safety as benchmarks for AI implementation, not only operational metrics.
Extend AI evaluation beyond technical validation to include purpose, context, and impact, such as who benefits, who is excluded, and how personhood is affected.
Design AI-based scheduling systems to be flexible so staff can indicate preferred working patterns and availability and request days off.
Allow managers to retain final authority to override AI scheduling suggestions when equity or context calls for it.
Recalibrate performance dashboards so that ethically motivated overrides count as quality rather than delay.
Involve frontline workers in designing, selecting, and evaluating AI technologies.
Ensure equitable access to AI resources across units.
Position digital interfaces and screens in consultation spaces so practitioner and patient can view information together and to minimize intrusive alerts.
Provide reflective practice, mentoring, and peer support to help practitioners maintain person-centredness when using AI.

screen.reason: This is a critical reflection and conceptual commentary applying the Person-Centred Practice Framework to examine how AI can be implemented while preserving relational ethics and person-centred values.
